title: Goods for all
hookLine: private property is real, but the earth's goods are meant for everyone

cards: "The earth is the Lord's and the fulness thereof: the world, and all they that dwell therein." That's a psalm, in the Douay-Rheims. Now look around the room you're in.
The chair is yours. The phone is yours. Maybe the walls are yours, or the bank's.

Catholic teaching says those claims are real. You can own things, and nobody gets to just take them. But it also says that underneath every deed and receipt, there's an older claim, and it belongs to everyone.
The Church has a long, slightly clunky name for it.

teach.h: THE EARTH: A GIFT TO EVERYONE.
teach.b: The name is the universal destination of goods. Destination here means purpose: where the goods of the earth are meant to go. First, the gift.
The Catechism starts here: God entrusted the earth and its resources to the whole human race, to take care of them and enjoy their fruits.
The land, the water, the harvest were a gift to everyone before they were anyone's.

Second, property is real. The Church doesn't abolish ownership. The Catechism defends the right to private property: people need a measure of security, a home, the freedom to plan and provide for their families.
Owning things, rightly used, is good. Third, the two hold together. The right to private property, the Catechism says, does not do away with the original gift of the earth to all.

teach.h: YOU HOLD IT AS A STEWARD.
teach.b: So what you own, you hold as a kind of steward.
The Second Vatican Council puts it this way in Gaudium et Spes: a person should regard the things they lawfully possess as common in this sense, that they can benefit others as well as themselves.
Fourth, the early Church, which this path first met in year one.
In Acts, the believers in Jerusalem shared what they had, and the Douay-Rheims says that "all things were common unto them."

Catholic teaching doesn't require everyone to live that way, though religious orders live something like it. But it stands as a picture of where the goods of the earth are headed. So the question isn't, is this mine?
The question is, what is this for?

how: Catholics live out the universal destination of goods through almsgiving, parish sharing programs and food banks, lending and giving what sits unused, and, in religious orders, holding property in common.

games.q: what does “universal destination of goods” mean?
o: a rule that all property belongs to the state
the place where Church donations are sent
the earth's goods are meant to serve everyone

games.q: goods for all — tap the pairs.
p: purpose: where goods are meant to go
all things were common unto them

s: the Catechism defends the right to private property.
the Catechism says ownership doesn't cancel the earth's original gift to all
the right to property does not do away with the original gift of the earth to the whole human race.
Catholic teaching requires every family to hold all things in common
Acts gives a picture of sharing; religious orders live something like it, but it isn't required of everyone.

games.q: you own a car that sits in the driveway most days. a neighbor without one needs to get to a job interview. what does this teaching suggest?
o: it's your car; keep it in the driveway.
give the car away for good.
lend it: what you own is also for others.
games.why: the teaching keeps ownership real, and asks what it's for: things lawfully owned can benefit others as well as yourself.

practice: Go through your home in your mind, room by room, and notice what sits unused: a coat in the closet, tools in the garage, books on a shelf.
No guilt; just ask of each thing, what is this for, then pick one you could lend or give, and one person or group who could use it.
If you pray, thank God for what you have; if you don't, simply hold the thing and the person together.
